newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels reject offer of Zaire cabinet posts.
newsitem.headline: Rebels reject offer of Zaire cabinet posts.

text.p: Zairean rebels on Thursday rejected an offer of six ministries to join a government headed by Zaire's new Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi and headed for talks in South Africa.

Asked by reporters as he boarded a plane in the Zairean city of Goma for the talks if the rebel alliance would accept the posts reserved by Tshisekedi for them, Raphael Nghenda, rebel information commissioner, said "No."
Nghenda boarded the plane accompanied by Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs commissioner for the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
Earlier on Thursday Tshisekedi unveiled a cabinet in Kinshasa with no associates of President Mobutu Sese Seko and six ministries reserved for the rebels in the civil war.

Tshisekedi, giving details of the 26-member government at a news conference, said portfolios of foreign affairs, defence, budget, planning, foreign trade and agriculture were reserved for the rebel alliance.
The rebels have said they would not negotiate with Tshisekedi as prime minister and would only deal directly with Mobutu.
Tshisekedi on Thursday showered praise on Kabila, whose rebels have seized a quarter of Zaire and are targeting mainstay mining centres after launching a rebellion from the Rwandan border in October.

"Kabila has contributed to the return of legality. He merits the acclaim of our people," Tshisekedi said, adding that the rebel leader took up arms because of Mobutu's "violation of the decisions of the national conference".
But he said the civil war now had to stop.
"I don't see the war continuing. Too much Zairean blood has been shed. I will see my brother Kabila and discuss," he said.

Nghenda and Karaha later left for South Africa for the first face-to-face negotiations between's Zaire's warring sides. Witnesses said rebel leader Kabila left Goma by air earlier on Thursday for an undisclosed destination ahead of the talks.
Diplomatic sources said on Wednesday Kabila was expected in Zimbabwe to seek the support of President Robert Mugabe and his influence within the OAU before the talks in South Africa.
A diplomatic source said Kabila was likely to be targeting other southern African leaders for understanding of his campaign to oust Mobutu.
